cards.body: A gas engine is a controlled explosion machine repeating four strokes: suck in air and fuel, squeeze it, spark it (bang!), blow out the exhaust. Hundreds of times per minute, in every cylinder.
cards.title: Suck, squeeze, bang, blow

cards.body: Torque is twisting force — what shoves you back in your seat off the line. Horsepower is how fast the engine sustains work — what keeps you accelerating at speed. Torque launches, horsepower cruises.
cards.title: Horsepower vs. torque, finally

cards.body: Why engines have multiple cylinders: one cylinder firing is a punch; eight firing in sequence is a purr. More cylinders means smoother power and more total bang per revolution — at the cost of fuel.
Listen to your engine. You don't need to be a mechanic to notice change — new knocking, whining, or grinding means something shifted. Catching it early is almost always cheaper than catching it late.

cards.explain: Suck (intake), squeeze (compression), bang (power), blow (exhaust) — the four-stroke cycle.
cards.q: The four strokes of a gas engine are…

choices: The spark ignites the mix and drives the piston down
questions.explain: The bang is the only stroke that makes power — the other three just set it up and clean up.
questions.q: What happens during the power stroke?

questions.explain: Torque twists. It's measured in lb-ft or Nm, and it's what you feel launching off a light.
Cylinders firing in sequence smooth out the power pulses — at the price of more fuel burned.

choices: Sustaining speed and acceleration at pace
questions.explain: Torque gets you moving; horsepower keeps you pulling hard at highway speed.

choices: Get it checked soon — early is cheaper
questions.explain: New noises mean something changed. Early diagnosis is cheap; late diagnosis is an engine rebuild.
questions.q: A new knocking sound from the engine means…

flashcards.back: Twisting force — what launches you off the line.
How fast the engine sustains work — what holds speed.
More cylinders firing in sequence = smoother, stronger power delivery.

cards.body: Low gears multiply torque for getting moving; high gears trade torque for speed once you're rolling. That's why first gear screams at 30 and fifth purrs at 100 — same engine, different leverage.
cards.title: Gears are leverage

cards.body: Pressing the pedal squeezes brake pads against spinning rotors, turning motion into heat. That's why brakes fade on long descents — overheated pads grip less. Downshifting (engine braking) saves them.
cards.title: How brakes actually stop you

cards.body: Tire pressure: the free upgrade. Under-inflated tires waste fuel, wear unevenly, and handle worse. The correct pressure is on the driver's door sticker — not the tire sidewall, which shows the maximum. Check monthly; it takes 2 minutes.
Tread tells the truth. Stick a coin in the tread — if you can see the top of the head, the tire is too worn for wet roads. Uneven wear across the tire also diagnoses alignment problems.

choices: It multiplies torque for getting moving
cards.explain: First gear is a torque multiplier for launching. High revs at low speed is exactly what it's for.
cards.q: Why does first gear rev high at low speed?

choices: Turning motion into heat via friction
questions.explain: Friction converts speed into heat — which is also why hard braking makes rotors glow on track cars.
Heat is the enemy of friction. Long descents cook the pads — downshift and let the engine help.
The sidewall shows the tire's maximum, not your car's spec. The door sticker is the answer.
questions.q: Where is your car's correct tire pressure?

choices: Downshifting to slow without the brakes
questions.explain: A lower gear makes the engine resist the wheels — free braking that saves your pads.
Tires should wear evenly. Bald edges or centers spell alignment or pressure issues.

flashcards.back: Low gears = torque for launching; high gears = efficiency at speed.
Overheated pads grip less — common on long descents; downshift to help.
On the driver's door sticker, not the tire sidewall. Check monthly.
Coin in the tread — visible head top means too worn for wet roads.

cards.body: Oil lubricates, cools, and cleans. Old oil turns to sludge and starves parts. Check the dipstick monthly, and change it per your manual — usually 8,000–12,000 km on modern synthetics, not the old 5,000 km myth.
cards.title: Oil is the engine's blood

cards.body: Warning lights that actually matter: red means stop soon (oil pressure, overheating, brakes). Yellow means check soon (check engine, tire pressure). A flashing check-engine light means misfire — ease off the gas and get it checked now.
cards.title: Warning lights, decoded

cards.body: Jump-starting without the drama: red clamp to the dead battery's positive, red to the good battery's positive, black to the good battery's negative, black to unpainted metal on the dead car (not its battery). Start the good car, wait a minute, start the dead one. Remove in reverse order.

Find your mechanic before you need one. Ask friends, read reviews, and get a small job like an oil change done first to test the shop. A trusted mechanic found calmly beats a random one found in a panic — and always get a quote before work.

choices: Pull over safely and stop the engine soon
cards.explain: No oil pressure kills an engine in minutes. Red means stop; the repair bill for ignoring it is catastrophic.
cards.q: A red oil-pressure light comes on. You…

questions.explain: The 5,000 km rule is a leftover from conventional oil. Modern synthetics go much further — trust the manual.

choices: Misfire — ease off and get checked now
questions.explain: A steady light means 'check soon'; flashing means 'misfire happening now' — unburned fuel is cooking your catalytic converter.

choices: Unpainted metal on the dead car
questions.explain: The last connection can spark — keep it away from the battery, where hydrogen gas may linger.
questions.q: When jump-starting, the final black clamp goes to…

choices: Outdated for most modern synthetics — follow the manual
questions.explain: Oil chemistry improved; the old interval is marketing inertia. Your manual knows your engine.

choices: Test the shop with a small job before an emergency
questions.explain: An oil change reveals their honesty, pricing, and communication — before you're stranded and desperate.
questions.q: Smartest way to find a mechanic?

flashcards.back: Follow your manual — often 8,000–12,000 km on modern synthetics.
Red = stop soon. Yellow = check soon. Flashing check-engine = misfire, ease off now.
Red to dead +, red to good +, black to good −, black to dead car's metal. Reverse to remove.
Test with a small job first; always get quotes before work.
